newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's secularists set to win government vote.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's secularists set to win government vote.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz looked set to win parliamentary approval for his anti-Islamist alliance on Saturday and bring at least a temporary end to months of political turmoil.

Conservative Yilmaz was expected to clinch a confidence vote by at least 20 votes in the 550-seat assembly. He was boosted by a late defection from the rival conservative True Path Party, now in opposition.
"The only parliamentary solution that can be seen is a government formed by Mesut Yilmaz," said former central bank chief Yalman Toruner, who quit True Path to join Yilmaz's Motherland Party.

Deputies were scheduled to gather at 1500 (1200 GMT) for the vote in Yilmaz's left-right government, cobbled together two weeks ago to replace the Islamist-led coalition of fallen prime minister Necmettin Erbakan.
Yilmaz' efforts to prevent a planned Islamist return to power are backed by President Suleyman Demirel and the army, now taking a more active role in politics.
A Yilmaz aide said the generals had stepped back from preparing to oust against Erbakan when it became clear that the secularist politicians could get rid of the Islamists.
"Talk of forming the government prevented a coup," Motherland deputy chairman Yasar Dedelek told a news conference. "That is why we are announcing July 12 as a democracy festival."

The anti-Islamist generals had openly criticised Erbakan, NATO member Turkey's first Islamist leader, for failing to heed army warnings to curb Moslem activism. The brass also turned on the secularist True Path for cooperating with Erbakan.
Yilmaz was expected to sail through the balloting in the 550-member national assembly. "An easy vote," the Milliyet daily said in its front-page headline.
"The government...will win the parliamentary confidence ballot by at least 20 votes," the Yeni Yuzyil newspaper said.
Yilmaz's parliamentary majority could be widened by opposition MPs staying away from parliament in quiet protest at True Path leader Tansu Ciller's ties to the Islamists.
The Turkish press named nine deputies whom it said would not turn up for the vote, thus aiding Yilmaz who needs only a simple majority of those attending the session.
Yilmaz and his two government partners have 217 MPs. They also expect the support of 49 other left-wing deputies, two rightists and 17 of the independents in the 550-seat assembly.
Ranged against Yilmaz are 157 Islamists, eight far-rightists and -- at least on paper -- 98 conservative True Path MPs.
Two MPs resigned True Path on Friday in a further blow to Ciller, who became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993.
She upset the secularists establishment by going into coalition with the Islamists last year and now faces the resurrection of old corruption allegations against her and her businessman husband.
Yilmaz has promised to introduce anti-Islamist legislation, particularly on education, and take Turkey closer to the European Union.
He has recently shown signs of backtracking on a promise to hold early elections next year, well before polls are due in the year 2000.
A key left-wing party warned it could withdraw its support for Yilmaz if he does not push elections legislation though parliament before a recess later this month.
"If there is no election law before the holiday we will reconsider our position," the Hurriyet daily quoted senior Republican People's Party MP Adnan Keskin as saying.
